analysis.investment_thesis: 3B Films fails both Magic Formula tests decisively: an earnings yield of ~2.5% (inverse of P/E 39.5) is far below my 6% floor, and a 0.17% ROE signals near-zero return on capital. This is neither cheap nor a good business — the exact opposite of what the Magic Formula seeks.
key_strengths: High promoter skin-in-the-game at 69.97% aligns incentives
Operates in a growing packaging/CPP-CPE films niche
Small market cap (INR 43 Cr) leaves room for operating leverage if scale comes
key_risks: ROE of 0.17% implies ROIC is near zero — capital-destructive economics
P/E 39.5 = earnings yield ~2.5%, expensive relative to tiny earnings base
Commodity CPP/CPE films is capital-intensive with weak pricing power
red_flags: Earnings yield ~2.5% is below my 6% avoid threshold
ROE 0.17% — effectively no return on shareholder capital
Zero DII ownership suggests no institutional conviction
Small, recently-listed BSE SME-style float with thin data history
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula ranks companies by earnings yield (EBIT/EV) and return on capital. 3B Films flunks both. With P/E at 39.5, earnings yield is roughly 2.5% — you could earn more in a risk-free government bond. ROE of 0.17% is essentially a rounding error; even if EBIT margins are modestly better than net margins, the return on capital for a CPP/CPE film manufacturer cannot plausibly clear my 20% threshold when ROE is this anemic. This is the textbook opposite of "cheap and good" — it is expensive and mediocre.

Packaging films is a commodity business with heavy capex, which punishes ROIC; scale leaders earn mid-teens returns, and sub-scale players like 3B (INR 43 Cr market cap) typically earn far less. I have no interest in paying 40x earnings for a business that generates negligible returns on the capital invested. The systematic, unemotional answer from my framework: avoid. A score of 1 reflects that both Magic Formula inputs are near the bottom of the distribution.
